report:
**Conclusion: The claim is well-supported by evidence — your view that it is false is not supported by the literature.**

Multiple observational studies and meta-analyses consistently show that bystander hands-only (chest-compression-only) CPR is associated with higher survival rates after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) compared to no bystander CPR. The evidence is strong and consistent:

1. **SOS-KANTO study (Lancet, 2007):** A nationwide Japanese observational study found that bystander chest-compression-only CPR was associated with better outcomes than conventional CPR and, by extension, far better than no CPR. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17368153/))

2. **BMJ nationwide study:** A population-based observational study comparing chest-compression-only CPR to conventional CPR by laypeople found comparable or superior outcomes for compression-only CPR, and both were superior to no CPR. ([BMJ](https://www.bmj.com/content/342/bmj.c7106))

3. **Meta-analysis (PMC):** A meta-analysis concluded that dispatcher-assisted chest-compression-only bystander CPR is associated with improved survival in adult OHCA patients compared to conventional CPR (and both outperform no CPR). ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2987687/))

4. **Time-to-CPR analysis (PubMed, 2025):** A recent study confirmed that earlier bystander CPR — at various time thresholds — is associated with higher survival compared to no bystander CPR. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40015622/))

**Evidence against the claim (your side):** I found no credible studies showing that bystander hands-only CPR provides no survival benefit over no CPR. The only nuance in the literature is that the *quality* of CPR matters — ineffective compressions may not improve survival (Semantic Scholar/Gallagher et al.). Additionally, one NEJM dispatcher-instruction trial found no *overall* statistically significant survival increase, though there was a trend toward benefit. ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0908993))

**Bottom line:** The overwhelming weight of evidence supports that bystander hands-only CPR improves survival after OHCA compared to doing nothing. The claim appears to be true, not false.
